stances.claim: Dr. Ty's commitment to donate 10% of his total wealth to philanthropy -- rather than the corporate norm of a maximum 2% of net income -- represented an extraordinary philanthropic threshold, one of the largest single private commitments in PH business history because of the absolute size of his fortune.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative-norm framing (10% personal wealth vs 2% corporate ceiling)

stances.claim: Dr. Ty's character was defined by humility, patience, and quiet attentiveness -- exemplified by his side-chair presence during multi-day Outstanding Teachers interviews, his never-intruding-but-listening stance, and his trust-based instruction to CJ to accept a competing BPI directorship despite Metrobank conflict ('I fully trust you. I know you will never reveal any business secret').

Dr. Ty's faith -- though never flaunted -- manifested in concrete acts: building the Mary the Queen Catholic Church in Nanjing as thanksgiving for the success of Metrobank's Chinese branches, becoming one of the largest donors to the Manila Cathedral renovation, and ultimately inheriting (per scripture) 'a dwelling place in heaven for the humble and meek.'

Dr. Ty's continuing influence operates in two registers: spiritually he is 'a free spirit capable of being with us on earth, watching us and inspiring us to be the best of what we can be'; institutionally his achievements, principles, and values are to be constantly remembered, personified, and championed by those who admired him.

notable_anecdotes: Dr. Ty's 20-year-prior bedside presence during Search for the 10 Outstanding Teachers interviews -- 'During several hours of interviews lasting two days, he was always present on a side chair, patiently listening but never intruding in the proceedings. At that time, he was the active chairman of his conglomerate, yet he found precious time to listen to the long interviews' -- the column's signature character-illustrating detail.

Dr. Ty's response to the Ayala BPI invitation: 'Please accept the offer. I fully trust you. I know you will never reveal any business secret, whether of Metrobank or of BPI or of anyone' -- the most compact single-quote demonstration of Dr. Ty's trust-based ethos.

Dr. Ty's home visit explaining the 10% commitment: 'God had been kind to him because all his business ventures have been successful. In thanksgiving, he wanted to donate 10 percent of his wealth to philanthropy' -- capturing the spiritual motivation behind the largest single philanthropic commitment.

Dr. Shoichiro Toyoda's matching P1 billion gift after CJ advised him of Dr. Ty's Toyota Motor Philippines School of Technology endowment -- a Japanese-PH philanthropic collaboration triggered by a single CJ communication.

Dr. Ty's appointment of CJ to succeed the late Cory Aquino as Metrobank Foundation board chair after Aquino's August 1, 2009 death -- the most institutionally significant succession recorded in the column.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban summarizes the eulogy he delivered on the evening of November 24, 2018 -- the first night of Dr. George S. K. Ty's wake -- directing readers to cjpanganiban.com for the full text. He acknowledges hesitancy to speak first when the family and Metrobank Group officers had known Dr. Ty far longer, and chooses to share personal stories illustrating Dr. Ty's principles. He recounts meeting Dr. Ty about twenty years earlier when invited to join (and later chair) the board of judges for the Metrobank Foundation's 'Search for the 10 Outstanding Teachers,' during which Dr. Ty -- then active chairman of the conglomerate -- sat patiently on a side chair throughout multi-day interviews without ever intruding. After CJ's retirement from the judiciary, Dr. Ty invited him to become a Senior Adviser of Metrobank and a board member of the Metrobank Foundation, eventually succeeding the late Cory Aquino as board chair after her August 1, 2009 death. When Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala invited CJ to BPI, Dr. Ty told him directly: 'Please accept the offer. I fully trust you. I know you will never reveal any business secret, whether of Metrobank or of BPI or of anyone' -- the column's compact demonstration of trust-based ethos. He recounts Dr. Ty's home visit explaining his commitment to donate 10% of his wealth to philanthropy in thanksgiving for his business success -- an extraordinary commitment given that he was one of the country's richest, and that corporations typically give only a maximum 2% of net income. From this commitment, P1 billion initially established the nonprofit Toyota Motor Philippines School of Technology focused on science and technology to eradicate extreme poverty, with Dr. Shoichiro Toyoda (retired Toyota Japan chair) matching the gift with another P1 billion after CJ informed him. Despite never flaunting his faith, Dr. Ty built the Mary the Queen Catholic Church in Nanjing, China, in thanksgiving for the success of his Chinese Metrobank branches, and became one of the largest donors to the Manila Cathedral renovation. Panganiban closes with the scriptural assurance that 'our Father reserved a dwelling place in heaven for the humble and meek' and that Dr. Ty is now 'a free spirit capable of being with us on earth -- watching us and inspiring us to be the best of what we can be.'
